title: Security Groups vs Network ACLs
intro: AWS has two firewalls. Security groups attach to instances and are stateful: replies are allowed automatically. Network ACLs attach to subnets and are stateless: every packet is checked in both directions. Most VPC 'it just times out' problems are one of these two. This tutorial audits and tightens them.

steps.prompt: Audit: find every security group with a rule open to the whole internet (0.0.0.0/0).
steps.fake_output:
GroupId                 GroupName   Protocol  Port   Source
sg-0a1a2a3a4a5a6a7a8    web-sg      tcp       443    0.0.0.0/0
sg-0b1b2b3b4b5b6b7b8    legacy-db   tcp       5432   0.0.0.0/0
steps.explanation: web-sg (443) is expected. legacy-db exposes postgres to the internet.
steps.why: Filtering on ip-permission.cidr turns a manual review of hundreds of groups into one query. Anything other than 80/443 open to 0.0.0.0/0 needs an explanation. Exposed databases and SSH are among the most common findings in real breach reports.

steps.prompt: Replace legacy-db's rule: first revoke 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0 on sg-0b1b2b3b4b5b6b7b8.
steps.why: Before revoking, check who legitimately connects (VPC Flow Logs or the application config), or you replace a security hole with an outage. Here the only real clients are the app servers.

steps.prompt: Allow 5432 on sg-0b1b2b3b4b5b6b7b8 only from members of the app servers' security group sg-0c1c2c3c4c5c6c7c8.
expected_commands: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0b1b2b3b4b5b6b7b8 --protocol tcp --port 5432 --source-group sg-0c1c2c3c4c5c6c7c8
steps.explanation: Only instances in the app security group can reach the database.
steps.why: Referencing a security group instead of a CIDR follows the servers as they scale: new app instances get access automatically and nothing else does, even if IPs change. This is the standard pattern for any internal tier (app to database, load balancer to app).

steps.prompt: Now the stateless layer: show the network ACL for subnet subnet-0aa11bb22cc33dd44.
steps.fake_output:
NetworkAclId: acl-0f0e0d0c0b0a09080 (public-nacl)
INBOUND   Rule  Proto  Ports        Source       Action
          100   tcp    443          0.0.0.0/0    ALLOW
          110   tcp    1024-65535   0.0.0.0/0    ALLOW
          *     all    all          0.0.0.0/0    DENY
OUTBOUND  Rule  Proto  Ports        Destination  Action
          100   all    all          0.0.0.0/0    ALLOW
          *     all    all          0.0.0.0/0    DENY
steps.explanation: Inbound allows 443 and the ephemeral range; outbound allows everything.
steps.why: Rules are evaluated lowest number first, and the first match wins. Inbound 1024-65535 exists for the replies to connections the instances open (package downloads, API calls). Remove it and outbound connections from this subnet silently break. mystery-aws-004 shows the mirror-image mistake on outbound.

steps.prompt: Block a scanner at 198.51.100.7 from the whole subnet, ahead of the allow rules: add inbound rule 90 denying all traffic from 198.51.100.7/32 on acl-0f0e0d0c0b0a09080.
steps.explanation: Rule 90 is evaluated before 100, so that IP is dropped before any allow rule matches.
steps.why: This is what NACLs are good for: coarse, subnet-wide, explicit DENY rules. Security groups can't deny at all, they can only allow. Keep NACLs simple and put fine-grained policy in security groups; every stateless rule you add is another place replies can be dropped.
